h1: How to split a marketing budget between SEO, paid and social — in rupees
metaTitle: How to Split a Marketing Budget: SEO, Paid, Social
metaDescription: Every budget page sizes SEO alone. This one gives the split in rupees at four budget levels, and names the total below which splitting buys nothing.
answer: Below roughly ₹1,00,000 a month in total, don't split at all — fund one channel properly. From ₹1,00,000 to ₹2,25,000, run two. All three become viable at about ₹2,50,000 and up, once you budget ad spend as a separate line from the fees that manage it.
takeaways: Percentage-of-revenue rules are borrowed from American budgets. Work backwards from what a customer is worth instead.
**Three ways is the most common mistake at small budgets.** Three underfunded channels lose to one funded one, every time.
Fees and media are separate lines. A ₹1,50,000 budget with ₹75,000 of fees has ₹75,000 of spend, not ₹1,50,000.
The earliest honest reallocation decision is about **90 days** for organic and **4–6 weeks** for paid, and only if paid had enough conversions to learn from.

sections.h2: Why percentage-of-revenue rules don't survive an Indian P&L
body: You'll be told to spend 5–10% of revenue on marketing. That number comes from American consumer businesses with American gross margins, and it breaks in two directions here.

A ₹4 crore B2B services firm at 7% gets ₹2.3 lakh a month, which is a real budget and probably more than it needs, because it might only be chasing forty buyers in the whole country. A ₹4 crore D2C brand on 30% gross margin gets the same ₹2.3 lakh, which after ad spend funds almost no owned marketing at all. Same rule, opposite answers, and neither is derived from anything the business actually needs.

Work it backwards instead. What is a customer worth to you over a year? How many more do you want? What have you historically paid to acquire one? Multiply, then compare that number to what you can afford. If the answer is smaller than the fees for one competent channel, the honest conclusion isn't a clever split — it's that you're not ready to outsource marketing yet.

callout.title: Read the second and third columns together
callout.body: Founders routinely quote a budget that turns out to be the fee, or the spend, but never both. "We've got ₹1,50,000 for marketing" means ₹99,000 of fees and ₹51,000 of media — or ₹40,000 of fees and ₹1,10,000 of media. Those are different plans with different outcomes. Decide which one you mean before you take a single call.

sections.h2: Below ₹1,00,000 a month, concentrating beats splitting
body: This is the unpopular part, and it costs us money to say it, because splitting a small budget three ways is how an agency sells three line items instead of one.

Every channel has a floor. Below about ₹40,000 a month, SEO buys a fraction of a person's attention and no link work worth the name. Below about ₹30,000, organic social is a posting schedule rather than a plan. And paid has the hardest floor of the three: an auction sets your cost, not your ambition, and [higher bids don't guarantee a better position](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6366577) — relevance and quality move it too. With too little spend you never accumulate enough conversions to tell a good campaign from a lucky week.

So ₹90,000 split ₹30,000 / ₹30,000 / ₹30,000 buys three things below their floor. The same ₹90,000 on one channel clears it comfortably. The second channel is the reward for the first one working, not a hedge against it failing.

Which channel? The one closest to how people already buy from you. If they search for what you sell, start with search. If they discover what you sell, start with paid social. There's a longer argument in [Google Ads vs SEO](/compare/google-ads-vs-seo), and a cautionary one in [why Indian D2C brands overspend on ads](/journal/why-indian-d2c-brands-overspend-on-ads).

sections.h2: Budget the fee and the spend as two separate lines
body: Media is the only part of a marketing budget that a third party can raise without asking you. Keeping it in its own line is what makes that visible.

Google Ads works off an average daily budget, and the monthly ceiling is [30.4 times that daily number](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6385083) — 365 divided by 12. So ₹60,000 a month of intended spend is a ₹1,973 daily budget, and any day can run over as long as the month doesn't. If you've mentally budgeted ₹60,000 and see ₹2,400 spent on a Tuesday, nothing is broken.

Two rules we'd apply to any agency, including us. Media is billed at cost with no markup — a percentage-of-spend fee quietly pays the agency more for spending more of your money. And the ad account stays in your name, so the invoices, the history and the audiences are yours. Our own prices sit on the [pricing page](/pricing) with spend excluded from every one of them.

callout.title: The all-in quote
callout.body: "₹2,00,000 a month, everything included" is not a budget, it's a hiding place. You cannot tell what the work costs, what the media costs, or what margin sits on the media. Ask for the two numbers separately before you compare it to anything. Any agency that won't separate them has told you why.

sections.h2: When to move money between channels
body: The temptation is to reallocate monthly, which mostly reallocates noise. The two channels run on different clocks and deserve different review windows.

Paid can be judged in four to six weeks, but only if it produced enough conversions to be judged — a campaign with nine conversions in a month tells you nothing you'd bet on. If volume is that low, the honest read is that the budget is too small for the channel, not that the channel failed.

Organic is slower and Google says so plainly: some changes take hours, [others take several months](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide). Ninety days is the earliest fair read, and what you're reading at day 90 is impressions and rankings for your target queries, not revenue. Cutting an SEO budget in month two is paying for the setup and cancelling before the delivery.

So: review paid monthly and act on it quarterly; review organic quarterly and act on it twice a year. Move money when a channel is starved rather than failing — those look identical on a dashboard and are opposite problems. And if you're deciding between spending more and spending better, [what SEO costs for a small business](/cost/seo-cost-for-small-business) has the version of this argument for tighter budgets.

faqs.q: How much of my marketing budget should go to SEO?
faqs.a: At small budgets, potentially all of it — if search is how your buyers find you. Percentages only start being useful above about ₹1,50,000 a month, where a rough half to fees for organic and half to media is a defensible starting point you then adjust on evidence.

faqs.q: What's the minimum viable marketing budget in India?
faqs.a: Around ₹40,000 a month of fees for one channel done properly, or roughly ₹75,000 total once you add media to a paid channel. Below that you're buying fractions of people's attention. It's often better to do one thing yourself for six months than to fund three at a tenth each.

faqs.q: Should ad spend be part of the agency fee?
faqs.a: No. Keep them as separate lines and pay media at cost with no markup. A percentage-of-spend arrangement rewards the agency for spending more of your money, and an all-in number hides both the fee and the margin on the media.

faqs.q: Is it better to split between SEO and ads or do one well?
faqs.a: One well, until roughly ₹1,00,000 a month in total. Each channel has a floor below which it can't compound, and a split budget usually funds three efforts beneath their floors. Add the second channel when the first one is working, not as insurance against it not working.

faqs.q: How often should I rebalance the split?
faqs.a: Review paid monthly and act quarterly. Review organic quarterly and act about twice a year. Reallocating faster than the channel's own feedback loop mostly moves money in response to noise, and organic in particular punishes stop-start funding.

faqs.q: Does the split change for a D2C brand?
faqs.a: Yes, and the order is nearly reversed. D2C usually has to buy discovery first, so paid social gets the first rupee. The mistake is stopping there — brands that never start organic keep renting every sale, and their blended acquisition cost rises every year.
